passage: From the flat below, you hear things. Last Sunday I was watering plants on the balcony when Urmila's voice came down through the window: "Darshan, it's a two-line email. How can it take you an hour? Honestly, you're hopeless." There were guests in their living room, I could tell from the extra chappals outside the door. Nobody laughed. Darshan said something too low for me to catch, and then a chair scraped. Later I saw Urmila alone on the stairs, scrolling on her phone without really looking at it, jaw tight. Her mother had mentioned that morning that Darshan got the coaching seat. I can't say what is in Urmila's head. But the two of them used to race up those stairs together, and now they climb one at a time, a floor apart.

qa.q: Where was the neighbour when Urmila's voice came through the window?
qa.a: The neighbour was on the balcony, watering plants, in the flat below.

qa.q: What might Urmila be feeling as she sits alone on the stairs?
qa.a: Perhaps something uneasy under the scorn, such as envy or worry about her own results. Her tight jaw and unseeing scrolling suggest she is not at ease, though the neighbour cannot be sure.

qa.q: What could Urmila try instead of calling Darshan hopeless?
qa.a: She could notice that mocking Darshan is pushing Darshan away, ask herself what she envies or fears, and talk with Darshan privately.

qa.q: How might Darshan have experienced the remark in front of the guests?
qa.a: Being called hopeless with guests present is likely embarrassing and hurtful. The low reply and the scraping chair suggest Darshan wanted to leave the room.

grounding: Urmila voices contempt for her sibling in front of others, seen by a neighbour who cannot know her inner state.

"Karthik, you can't even boil an egg? Seriously?" Sahil laughed, loud enough for the cousins in the hall to hear. "My brother, the genius."
Karthik put the pan down and walked out. The cousins went quiet.
Later, Papa found Sahil on the balcony. "That was the third time today."
"He's lazy, Papa. He sleeps till ten. He never studies. And everyone still loves him."
"Hmm. And what bothers you most about that?"
"Nothing. I just think he's useless."
Papa waited.
"Fine," Sahil muttered. "He gets to be easy-going and I have to be the serious one. I'm scared if I relax for one day, I'll fall behind. And he never seems scared of anything."
"So it's not really about eggs."
Sahil laughed, but it came out wrong. "No." He looked through the glass at Karthik, alone with his phone. "He doesn't talk to me anymore. I guess I did that."

qa.q: Where did Papa find Sahil later?
What was Sahil really feeling beneath the insults?
qa.a: He felt envious of Karthik's easy-going life and afraid of falling behind if he ever relaxed.

qa.q: What would you advise Sahil to do next?
qa.a: Apologise to Karthik, especially for mocking him in front of the cousins, and try talking to him about something he likes instead of criticising.

qa.q: How does Karthik likely see Sahil's jokes?
qa.a: To Karthik they feel humiliating, especially in front of the cousins, so he walks out and has stopped talking to his brother.

grounding: A teen who calls his brother useless realises contempt has shut down their closeness and that it hides his own envy and fear.

passage:
I said it in front of his friends. That's the part I keep coming back to.
Last winter my brother Naveen failed his pre-boards in two subjects. When his friends came over, I said, "Don't ask Naveen for help with anything, he's too dumb to pass maths." They laughed. He didn't. He went red and quietly shut his door.
For weeks I told myself I was just being honest. Naveen really was wasting time on his guitar.
It was Ammachi who asked me, "Sabina, why does his failing make you so angry?" I didn't have an answer that night. Later, I did. I was scared. Our parents already lean on me for everything. If Naveen failed, I'd be the only one they could count on, and I didn't want that weight.
I apologised in March. He accepted it, sort of. He still doesn't show me his songs.

qa.q: How many subjects did Naveen fail in his pre-boards?
What was Sabina afraid of, underneath the anger at Naveen?
qa.a: Sabina was scared of carrying the family's hopes alone if Naveen failed, and the fear came out as contempt.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could help rebuild closeness now?
qa.a: Mocking Naveen in front of his friends shut him out; Sabina could keep showing respect, like asking to hear one of his songs without judging.

qa.q: What is it like for Naveen when Sabina mocks him?
qa.a: He feels humiliated in front of his friends and shuts his door, and he still keeps his songs private from Sabina.

grounding: A teen who called a brother dumb in front of others realises the contempt hid fear and has damaged their closeness.
